summary.text: Probiotics are live microorganisms intended to support a host's health, found in foods like yogurt, cheese and nattō or in capsules.
Many claimed benefits lack substantial scientific support, and as of 2019 numerous health-claim applications from European supplement makers were rejected for insufficient evidence.
Benefits shown for one strain are strain-specific and cannot be extrapolated to other strains.

facts.label: First discovered
facts.value: Lactobacillus bulgaricus, found in Bulgarian yoghurt in 1905

facts.label: Counted in
facts.value: Colony forming units, the number of viable microorganisms

facts.label: Typical dose
facts.value: One to ten billion CFU per dose

items.prompt: A company shows its own bacterium eased constipation. A rival sells a different bacterium and borrows the claim. What is wrong?

options.label: Constipation is the one condition probiotics can never help
Only capsules can carry a claim, never yogurt
Such benefits are strain-specific and cannot be extrapolated to other strains
Claims are allowed only if the bacterium is dead

items.explain: The claimed benefits are strain-specific, so a result for one strain cannot be assumed for another.

items.prompt: A shopper buys a capsule with ten times as many live cells as usual, expecting ten times the benefit. What is likely?

options.label: No extra benefit, and possibly bloating, gas and diarrhea
Ten times the benefit, since more cells means more effect
No change at all, since the cells die in the stomach
Fewer side effects, because the cells crowd each other out

items.explain: A higher number of CFUs does not provide additional probiotic effects and may cause digestive discomfort such as bloating, gas and diarrhea.

items.prompt: Why did the European Commission ban the word "probiotic" from packaging?

options.label: The microorganisms were shown to be unsafe for everyone
One company had trademarked the word
The products were found to contain no live cells
It misleads consumers into thinking a health benefit is proven when it is not

items.explain: The labeling misleads consumers to believe a health benefit is provided when no scientific proof exists of that effect.

items.prompt: The FDA treats probiotics as generally recognized as safe. What does that tell a buyer?

options.label: They are proven to improve health
They are safe when used as intended, but this does not prove they work
They are safe for every person, including premature infants
They are approved to treat disease

items.explain: The GRAS designation supports safety when used as intended but does not establish effectiveness or specific health benefits.

items.prompt: A hospital is deciding who should take extra care with probiotics. Which patient is at higher risk?

options.label: A person with a weakened immune system
A healthy teenager who eats yogurt every day
An adult who just ran a marathon
A person recovering from a mild cold

items.explain: People with immunodeficiency, among others, may be at higher risk for adverse events.

items.prompt: A household keeps vegetables edible through winter by letting them sour in a crock. Why do societies rely on this?

options.label: It sterilizes the food so no living microbes remain
It requires constant refrigeration to work
Souring by acid fermentation is a practical method with low cost and energy needs
It works only on milk and never on vegetables

items.explain: Acid fermentation remains one of the most practical methods of preserving fresh vegetables because of its low cost and energy requirements.

paragraphs.heading: Live microbes taken for health
paragraphs.text: Probiotics are live microorganisms meant to support or improve the health of the host that takes them. They are widely used in both people and animals. The word names the microbes themselves, but people take them in many forms: yogurt, cheese, fermented foods such as nattō, or capsules holding one strain or a set mix of strains.

paragraphs.heading: A Bulgarian yogurt story
paragraphs.text: The first probiotic found was a strain in Bulgarian yogurt called Lactobacillus bulgaricus. Bulgarian physician and microbiologist Stamen Grigorov discovered it in 1905. The modern idea is usually credited to Élie Metchnikoff, a Russian Nobel Prize winner. Around 1907 he proposed that Bulgarian peasants who ate yogurt lived longer.

paragraphs.heading: Defining and measuring a dose
paragraphs.text: In 2001 the World Health Organization defined probiotics as live microbes that give the host a health benefit when taken in adequate amounts. Experts meeting in Canada in 2013 settled on a slightly adjusted version of that wording. Doses are counted in colony forming units (CFU), the number of living microbes in a product, and typical doses run from 1 to 10 billion CFU depending on the use. Taking more CFUs adds no extra probiotic effect and can bring bloating, gas and diarrhea.

paragraphs.heading: Probiotics on the plate
paragraphs.text: Live probiotic cultures turn up in fermented dairy, other fermented foods and foods with added probiotics. Lactic acid bacteria ferment food; they can stop it spoiling and can raise its nutritional value. Acid fermentation, like salting, remains a cheap, low-energy way to keep fresh vegetables, cereal gruels and milk-cereal mixes. Kimchi, for example, carries Leuconostoc, Weissella and Lactobacillus species, while kefir contains Lactobacillus acidophilus, Bifidobacterium bifidum and Streptococcus thermophilus, among others.

paragraphs.heading: Safe is not the same as proven
paragraphs.text: In the United States the FDA regards probiotics as generally recognized as safe (GRAS), which backs their safety when used as intended, but that label does not show they work. Many health claims lack substantial scientific support, for example that probiotics treat eczema or cure vaginal infections. Where a benefit is shown, it applies only to that strain and cannot be assumed for others. As of 2019 the European Food Safety Authority had rejected every health-claim petition from probiotic makers in Europe, for lack of evidence of cause and effect.

paragraphs.heading: Rules and risks
paragraphs.text: The European Commission banned the word probiotic on packaging, since it leads buyers to expect a health benefit that has not been proven. Canada requires any label using the word to carry a government-approved health claim about the specific microbe. In the United States the FDA and FTC have warned and punished makers whose labels claim to treat a disease. Premature babies, and people with immunodeficiency, short bowel syndrome or heart valve disease, may face a higher risk of harm. Rarely, in children with lowered immunity or critical illness, probiotics can lead to bacteria or fungi in the blood and then sepsis, which can be fatal.
